definition: Discursive means rambling from topic to topic; lacking a clear, direct structure.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word discursive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know discursive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The lecture was so discursive that students' notes wandered from beekeeping to tax law before ever touching the syllabus.
Loose is weaker than discursive: loosely organized writing still follows its subject, just casually, while discursive writing wanders away from the subject altogether.
Incoherent is stronger than discursive — incoherent writing has no traceable thread at all, while a discursive piece rambles yet can still be followed, detour by detour.

Rambling talk drifts on and on without direction, but each stretch of it still makes sense as you follow along. Discursive is its more formal cousin: writing or speech that wanders from topic to topic, losing the thread of its subject without ever losing plain sense.

Meandering means winding indirectly from point to point, the way a river takes the long way — slow, but connected the whole way. A discursive answer strays further: it leaves the route altogether, hopping between topics with no clear structure to bring it back.

Discursive means rambling from topic to topic; lacking a clear, direct structure.
The best man's toast began with how the couple met.
Four minutes in, it had detoured through his own college roommate troubles, a theory about parallel parking, and a story involving a borrowed kayak that never reached its point.
Guests kept lifting their glasses hopefully, only to lower them again.
The toast was warm, even funny in places — but so discursive that when he finally said 'to the happy couple,' half the room had forgotten whose wedding it was.
The toast's detours through roommates, parking theories, and kayaks — with no through-line back to the couple — show the topic-to-topic rambling that discursive names.
formal; critical of writing and speech

Marisol's cooking blog began as a recipe archive, but longtime readers know the recipes are the least of it.

A post titled 'Weeknight Lentil Soup' is typical: it opens with the soup, detours into her aunt's superstitions about salt, spends three paragraphs on a 1954 bus strike, and closes with thoughts on chipped bowls.
Critics call the style discursive, and Marisol cheerfully agrees — the wandering, she says, is the point.
Each digression is lucid on its own; the difficulty is only that the soup disappears for screens at a time.
Her editor once tried to trim a post back to its recipe.
Readers revolted, and the digressions returned the following week.
